title: Curricular Practical Training (CPT) Protocol Effective May 6, 2021
label: Not covered
text: Curricular Practical Training (CPT) Protocol Effective May 6, 2021 | International Student and Scholar Services | University of Colorado Boulder Skip to main content Search Enter the terms you wish to search for. This site All of Colorado.edu Other ways to search: Events Calendar Campus Map Advising Services MyISSS Portal Departmental Services Immigration Alerts & FAQs Curricular Practical Training (CPT) Protocol Effective May 6, 2021 Published:2/1/2021 2/1/2021 Curricular Practical Training (CPT) is a temporary training authorization for an “alternative work/study, internship, cooperative education, or any other type of required internship or practicum which is offered by sponsoring employers through cooperative agreements with the school.” ISSS is updating our Curricular Practical Training (CPT) protocol to ensure that CU Boulder maintains compliance with the Department of Homeland Security F-1 visa regulations and is more closely aligned with the CPT policies of our peer institutions. CPT must be an integral part of your major curriculum, supported by either a credit bearing internship class or required for your major for any CPT authorized for May 6, 2021 or later. You must meet one of the following requirements for CPT, which your major department must sign off on: Be enrolled in an internship course for credit that counts towards your degree. (Enrollment in the course must be concurrent with the training. For example, if the internship is in the summer, you must be enrolled in the internship course during the summer) or Your degree must require an internship and that requirement is clearly documented in the University Catalog . If you do not meet the requirements for the CPT protocol effective May 6, 2021, then you have the option to apply for pre-completion OPT for off-campus work authorization. Please review ISSS’s Pre-completion OPT webpage and ISSS Pre-Completion OPT Guide for information on pre-completion OPT. ISSS understands the impact this change in CPT protocol may have on our international students in F-1 status who would like to take advantage of off-campus training opportunities. However, this change is necessary in order to ensure both CU Boulder and our international students in F-1 status are in compliance with federal rules. ISSS encourages you to attend a CPT Workshop via zoom to learn more about the CPT Protocol Effective May 6th. All sessions take place online via Zoom . February 23, 2021 at 3:30 p.m. March 18, 2021 at 3:30 p.m. April 6, 2021 at 5 p.m. April 29, 2021 at 11 a.m. Further information regarding CPT, including frequently asked questions and answers, is available on the ISSS Curricular Practical Training (CPT) Protocol Effective May 6, 2021 webpage .

text: Groups Tied to Harvard Sue DHS Over New Limits on International Student Internships | The Harvard Crimson The Harvard Crimson Advertisement Advertisement News Groups Tied to Harvard Sue DHS Over New Limits on International Student Internships A coalition of higher education groups with ties to Harvard sued the Department of Homeland Security Monday over new restrictions on Curricular Practical Training for international students. | By E. Matteo Diaz By Sebastian B. Connolly and Summer E. Rose , Crimson Staff Writers A coalition of higher education groups sued the Department of Homeland Security Monday, alleging that two August directives restricting which internships international students can take part in on student visas had caused “irreparable harm” to students and institutions. In a 44-page filing in federal court in Massachusetts, lawyers for the plaintiffs argued that the DHS had engaged in “procedurally invalid” rulemaking reinterpreting the rules governing Curricular Practical Training — a program allowing international students to participate in internships and experiential learning opportunities — to allow it only for internships that every student in a degree program must complete to graduate. The Student and Exchange Visitor Program, which certifies schools to enroll international students, detailed the interpretation of the rule in two broadcast messages on Aug. 12 and 24. In the messages, SEVP officials framed the update as a reminder of existing policy — and warned that universities could lose their SEVP certification, which would bar them from hosting students on visas. The Aug. 12 message also warned that improper authorizations could expose individual school officials, not just their institutions, to “administrative or legal consequences.” In Monday’s suit, lawyers for the plaintiffs argued that the broadcasts are “impermissibly retroactive,” exposing those officials to “criminal prosecution” for past conduct that complied with the government’s position at the time. But in Monday’s filing, lawyers for the plaintiffs argued that the messages broke with more than 35 years of precedent in how the rule had been interpreted — and were an attempt to introduce new legislative rules without abiding by federal procedure governing administrative action. Harvard has ties to all four plaintiffs in the Monday suit: the Association of American Universities, Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, NAFSA: Association of International Educators, and the Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts. The University is a member of AAU, AICUM, and the Presidents’ Alliance, and staff in the Harvard International Office are NAFSA members. Harvard is among several universities to have halted CPT authorizations following the August messages. Five of its schools — Harvard College, Harvard Law School, Harvard Medical School, the Graduate School of Design, and the Graduate School of Arts and Sciences — no longer authorize CPT, and the HIO updated its website to reflect the new guidance. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology, University of Pennsylvania, and Wellesley College are among the schools that have paused authorization of CPT applications since the messages were issued. Get The Crimson in your inbox. Sign up The complaint asks a judge to “restore” the previous interpretation, which allowed students to use CPT for internships taken for academic credit, arguing that the change had already harmed students and schools. “Action is needed now,” the lawyers wrote. “Students have already lost critical internship and research opportunities for the current semester and institutions have had to scramble to determine how ongoing practicums, internships extended from last summer, and applications for future internships might be impacted.” In a separate motion filed Monday night, the plaintiffs asked the court to block DHS from enforcing the new interpretation while the case proceeds. A DHS spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment The August messages come after a series of federal moves to tighten restrictions on international students. In July, DHS announced a rule that would place a fixed four-year limit on student visas and restrict students’ ability to switch programs. Three of the plaintiffs in Monday’s complaint — the Presidents’ Alliance, NAFSA, and AICUM — are suing to block the rule. On Sept. 14, a day before the rule was set to take effect, a federal judge temporarily blocked it. The government has since appealed the ruling, and the case is ongoing. Advertisement Harvard is engaged in its own lawsuit over the Trump administration’s attempt in May 2025 to revoke its SEVP certification — a case that plaintiffs cited in their separate Monday memorandum seeking an injunction noting that a federal judge had recognized evidence that losing SEVP certification can “irreparably harm” a university. The judge in that case blocked the revocation with a preliminary injunction in June 2025. The government filed a stipulation in August 2025, saying it would decline to enforce the May ruling. —Staff writer Sebastian B. Connolly can be reached at [email protected] or on Signal at sbc.23. text: Higher education leaders file lawsuit against ICE over international student internship restrictions Skip to main content Higher ed leaders sue Trump administration over limitations on international student internships Print this Article View Comments The Moakley Federal Courthouse on Boston Harbor Lane Turner/Globe Staff A coalition of higher education leaders filed a lawsuit Monday in Boston challenging the federal government’s recent interpretation of an internship program for international students, which plaintiffs say will limit student access to work experience and weaken America’s edge in talent recruitment. The lawsuit comes in response to messages US Immigration and Customs Enforcement emailed to university administrators in August that abruptly shifted the requirements for Curricular Practical Training (CPT), a program that allows international students to participate in internships, co-ops, and other temporary work programs related to their studies. The messages declared that students will only be eligible for CPT if the work opportunity is a graduation requirement for all students in a particular degree program, regardless of citizenship. “This action is yet another attempt by the [Trump] administration to dissuade talented international students from continuing their education in America,” Rob McCarron, president of the Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts, one of the plaintiffs in the case, said in a statement. When contacted by The Boston Globe, an ICE spokesperson said the agency does not comment on pending litigation. According to statistics from ICE , 130,586 foreign students obtained work authorization through CPT in 2024. The top employers of CPT participants in that year included Amazon, Tesla, and Google. Some universities have already limited CPT authorizations ahead of the fall 2026 semester; Harvard University , Massachusetts Institute of Technology , Boston University , Tufts University , and Suffolk University are among the Massachusetts schools that have all temporarily paused most new and pending CPT authorization requests. All five schools are members of AICUM. Several schools in the University of California system, such as the University of California Berkeley , have paused their course-credit work experiences altogether. The Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, another plaintiff in the new case, claimed that some students have already lost work positions they secured months prior as a result of these institutional changes. McCarron, president of the independent colleges group, said the ICE messages have caused “substantial disruptions” on campuses across Massachusetts as schools were forced to abruptly readapt longstanding processes surrounding student work experiences. In the messages sent Aug. 12 and 24, ICE claims that the Student and Exchange Visitor Program has observed a rise in schools issuing CPT authorizations that violate the requirement that work experience to be an “integral part of an established curriculum.” While the text of the regulatory requirements for CPT has not changed, it seems ICE’s interpretation of the word “integral” has shifted. The ICE messages warned that any institution found in violation could be investigated and lose certification to enroll international students. The plaintiffs said the new interpretation of CPT requirements has left long-standing campus practices like co-op programs in limbo without allowing adequate time for schools to respond or take public comment. The lawsuit also alleges that the communications were sent directly to campus university designated school officials — the employees in charge of advising international students and ensuring the university’s compliance with law — and threatened them with institutional penalties and personal liability for allowing previous CPT practices to continue. The lawsuit includes a motion for a preliminary injunction to force the government to stop any changes to CPT immediately, and as long as the case is active. The Presidents’ Alliance and several other plaintiffs in the case previously sued the Department of Homeland Security over limits on how long international students can stay on certain visas; a case that is ongoing. Chloe Craft can be reached at chloe.craft@globe.com .

text: New federal CPT guidelines leave international students across the U.S. without work New federal CPT guidelines leave international students across the U.S. without work 1 month 1 week 2 days ago Friday, August 28 2026 Aug 28, 2026 August 28, 2026 1:04 PM August 28, 2026 in News Source: WBRZ By: WBRZ Staff Share: BATON ROUGE — Universities around the country were issued new guidelines on Monday regarding Curricular Practical Training programs, causing many students enrolled in programs to lose their jobs. CPTs allow students to obtain a part-time job in their area of study and are the only way many international students can legally work while in school. The new guidelines come as the Student and Exchange Visitor Program observed a rise in CPT authorizations that appear to violate regulatory requirements, which permit CPT only where the training is an integral part of an established curriculum. SEVP noted that several institutions throughout the country have described CPT as an optional practical training despite clear regulatory requirements. CPTs that are classified as optional would fail to meet the integral and required aspects for authorization under the new guidelines. It was also discovered that some institutions have not required all students enrolled in the same established curriculum to participate in practical training.
